spn_df_crows.description:
Take it, go on. It's a good bow, it's a better bow than I deserve, and I can't use it any more.

I'm Huntress Verrel, and I've been trying to shoot the crows of the Dead Field for a week. They don't die the way crows die. I hit them. I know I hit them. I've hit a bird at twice that distance in worse light every season since I was fourteen. They take it, and they look at me, and then they settle on the next fence-post down and wait for me to try again.

I've started flinching, and that's why you're getting the bow. A hunter who's begun to flinch is no use to anybody until she's seen somebody else do it right.

Go and clear the fence line. I'll watch, and then I'd like the bow back.
spn_df_crows.accept_text: Go to the fence line along the Dead Field. Take the bow, because I've stopped trusting it.
spn_df_crows.turn_in_text:
She takes the bow back and checks the string out of pure habit.

So it was the birds.

That's the best news I've had in a fortnight. I can work with a wrong bird. I was starting to think I'd have to go home.

spn_df_harrowers.description:
You'll have to come up to the loft if you want to talk. I don't go down after dark.

My name's Tobb, and I worked this field. I was the last one out when it went bad and the first one back when I couldn't stand being anywhere else, which I know says something about me, and I'd rather it wasn't said.

The scarecrows walk. I've watched them from this window for weeks. They come down off the posts at dark and go up and down the furrows the way we used to walk them, and at first light they're back on the frames.

I'm not frightened of them, quite. It's that they're doing it right, the spacing, the turns at the headland. Somebody taught them that, and the only people who knew it are the ones who used to work here. Get them out of the furrows.
spn_df_harrowers.turn_in_text:
I came down, for the first time after dark since the spring.

I stood in the middle of the field and there was nothing in it but me. That's what I wanted, and it's a good deal lonelier than I'd thought through.

spn_df_king.description:
Now I'll tell you what I was really doing out here with a bow I'd stopped trusting.

There's one in the field that rules the rest. It's taller than a man, with a straw crown on it, wrapped up in a farmer's shroud, and the others take their timing from it. I've watched the whole field turn at the headland because that thing turned.

I've shot it twice. Both were good hits, both in it, and it didn't go down and it didn't get angry. It looked at me, properly looked, for about as long as it takes to decide something.

And it's been coming a little closer to this fence every night since. I'd rather not be the thing it decided about. Put it down.
spn_df_king.turn_in_text:
Verrel lets out a breath she looks like she's been holding for a fortnight.

It stayed down.

I'll sleep in the open tonight, out by the fence, just to prove to myself I can. And tomorrow I'm going to shoot something ordinary and enjoy it enormously.

spn_df_ring.description:
It's a gold band, tarnished to brown, pecked out of a crow's nest in the fence line and dropped in the stubble.

It's a plain thing, with no stones and no pattern, the sort of ring bought by somebody who'd been saving for it rather than choosing it.

The inside is engraved, worn soft but perfectly legible:

T. and L., forever.

There's a farmhand sleeping in the Dead Field barn who gave his initial to half the stories in this valley, and a wife he doesn't talk about except by her stitching.
spn_df_ring.turn_in_text:
Tobb turns it over without putting it on.

This is Lenna's. She lost it in the harvest the year before the plague, and we went through that stubble on our hands and knees for two days.

She said a crow had it. I said crows don't take gold, they take shine, and she said that was the same thing to a crow and I was being difficult.

He closes his hand around it.

She was right. She was usually right.

spn_df_straw.description:
There's one more thing, and then I'll let you go, and I'd ask you to be careful how you look at me while I say it.

Every harrower has a charm sewn inside its coat, straw, bound in a cross, the old kind people put up for a good harvest. My wife made them. She made one for every hand on this farm every spring, and she was teased about it for years.

I know the stitching. I'd know it anywhere. She went round the outside twice and back through the middle, and nobody else in Silverpine does it that way.

Bring the charms back to me. I don't want them in those coats. I want them somewhere decent, where what she meant by them is still what they mean.
spn_df_straw.turn_in_text:
He goes through them one at a time, feeling the backs.

They're all hers.

I'll put them in the barn above the door, which is where she'd have hung them anyway if anyone had let her. And then I think I might go and stay at the Crossroads a while.

I've done what I came back to do. I'd got it into my head that I had to keep doing it forever.

spn_farmhand_locket.description:
It's a silver locket, pried out of the coat pocket of a risen farmhand. He carried it the way the seed sacks are carried, because carrying it was simply what he did.

It opens stiffly. There's no portrait inside, only a name scratched into the metal in a hand that wasn't a craftsman's:

Marta.

Under the name, folded small and gone brittle, is a lock of grey-brown hair. It's the same colour as the woman's at Olsen's Farthing, who has a husband that walks past her window at the same hour every night and never comes to the door.
spn_farmhand_locket.turn_in_text:
She takes it in both hands and sits down on the step.

He scratched that himself. He had no hand for letters and he wouldn't let the smith do it. He said it wouldn't count.

He was carrying it, all this time, out there, in the same pocket.

I'll say the cleric's rite tonight. I'll have this on when I do, and he can go, and I'll know that whatever was still walking out there had hold of the right thing.

spn_farthing_hounds.description:
Mind the fence. Don't put your hand on the fence.

I'm Gaffer Olsen. I kept hounds here for forty years, good ones, working dogs, and I'd have told anybody who asked that I knew every one of them better than I knew most people.

Since the plague they've kept me. They pace that fence all night. They don't bark. They pace, and they stop when I come to the window, and they wait for me to go back to bed. And the risen hands open the gate for them, because opening the gate was their job and nobody's told them the farm's finished.

I'm an old man who's frightened of his own dogs, and I'll say that out loud rather than dress it up. Deal with the hands, and deal with the pack.
spn_farthing_hounds.turn_in_text:
The yard's quiet.

I slept, the first full night since the plague came through. I'd forgotten what it does to a man's thinking to get a whole one.

spn_gate_hold.description:
I'm Gatewarden Ilsa. State your business or stand aside. No, don't, I can see what you are. Come here, you're useful.

This is the iron door of the Sepulcher. The dead are welcome through it. That's what the place is for, and I've no quarrel with anyone who walks up and asks.

My quarrel is with what follows them. The treants have come down off the ridge and the ghouls come in behind, and between them the approach has become a thing you have to fight your way along to reach a door that was built to be open.

I've held this gate a long time, and I've never once had to tell a newly risen soul to run the last stretch. Clear the approach.
spn_gate_hold.turn_in_text:
The approach is walkable.

Two came in this evening on their own feet, slowly, looking at everything the way they do. That's how it's supposed to go. That's the entire job.

spn_muckmaw.description:
It's in the deep pool, the one at the back that doesn't reflect anything.

There's something in it. It's old, older than the springs turning, I think, and that isn't a thing I say lightly. It took Hest in the spring and it took Dorn in the autumn, and both times there was no struggle at all. They were at the bank, and then they weren't.

The locals call it Muckmaw, which makes it sound like a story for children. I've let them keep calling it that, because the alternative is explaining to a patrol that there's something in my pools that eats a Forsaken without waking the water.

Kill it for me. I've run out of scouts and patience, in roughly that order.
spn_muckmaw.accept_text: Go to the Shadowspring Pools. It's in the deep pool at the back, the one with no reflection.
spn_muckmaw.turn_in_text:
Yaelis stands at the deep pool's edge for a long moment, which she hasn't done in a year.

It reflects now.

I'd never once seen the bottom of that. There's a cart down there, a whole cart, and I've no idea how long it's been in my pools.

spn_old_hob.description:
There's one more, and I've been putting it off since you got here.

Hob leads the pack. He's the oldest dog I ever had, and he was the best of them. He wasn't the quickest or the keenest nose, but he was the one you could leave with the stock and the one the children could pull about. He slept under that bench. You can still see where he wore the grass away.

He's out past the top gate now and the rest follow him, and I've had a season of telling myself that means something's left in him. There's nothing left. I've watched him work the fence, and there's nothing in it that was my dog.

Don't make it slow. That's the whole of what I'm asking.
spn_old_hob.accept_text: He's past the top gate, and he leads them. Don't make it slow.
spn_old_hob.turn_in_text:
Olsen is sitting on the bench when you come back.

It was quick, then, and I'm glad.

Forty years of dogs, and that one was the best of them. I'll have him under the bench where he used to lie. He's earned a spot a damn sight more than I have.

spn_olsens_seed.description:
Now for something that isn't killing, if you can stand it.

The hands are still carrying the seed, in their coat pockets, same as they did when there was sowing to do. They carry a sack each, because that was how my father ran it and I never saw reason to change it.

I want it back. I want to put one row in, up the near side where the drainage is decent, and see whether anything comes up.

I know what you're thinking, and you'd be right. Nothing's grown in Silverpine soil since the plague. But I've got a season's worth of nothing to do and a farm that's stopped being a farm, and with one row in I'm a man waiting to find out instead of a man who's finished.
spn_olsens_seed.turn_in_text:
He opens a sack and runs it through his fingers.

It's dry, and dry's the main thing, because dry seed keeps.

I'll put the row in on Thursday. Come back in the spring, and we'll both find out together.

spn_orchard_blight.description:
I'm Malwick, orchard-warden. It's a title I keep using because the alternative is admitting what I actually am now, which is a man who walked to the Sepulcher to ask for help with some apples.

Malden's Orchard hasn't borne fruit in years. The trees still drop, mind. Brown stuff, heavy, comes down in the night, and then it moves. It gets up off the grass and goes about the rows.

That's the shamblers. And where the windfall piles up and rots, the wasps have hived in it, so now you can't clear the one without going through the other. I've tried both orders.

Get the shamblers out of the rows and the wasps out of the rot. Then I can at least walk my own orchard, which is more than I've managed since spring.
spn_orchard_blight.turn_in_text:
I walked the long row, both ways, with no stick.

You'll think that's a small thing. I planted the long row.

spn_orchard_cores.description:
He sets a cut rotapple on the table between you.

Look at it, if you've got the stomach. There, at the middle. That's a seed-core, rotapple, black all through, dense as a stone and warm. It isn't warm from the sun. I've taken them out at first light in frost, and they were warm then.

Every shambler has one. That means they aren't rotting fruit that learned to walk. They're being seeded, and whatever's doing the seeding is putting something into each one that holds its heat.

Bring me the cores. There's a furnace at the end of the orchard that hasn't been lit since Malden's day, and I intend to light it, and put every one of them in it, and stand there until they're ash.
spn_orchard_cores.accept_text: They're at the heart of each shambler, black, dense and warm. You'll feel it.
spn_orchard_cores.turn_in_text:
The furnace is already roaring when you get back.

In they go.

Listen to that, they're spitting. Whatever's in those was never going to come out of that orchard on its own.

spn_orchard_graft.description:
Here's my proposition, and I've had two seasons to be sure of it.

Every tree in that orchard is rotted at the root, every one. I've dug up four to be certain, including the long row, and there's nothing to be reversed. The blight isn't in the fruit, it's in the ground, and the ground is going nowhere.

But the wood higher up is still clean in places, the high boughs, the new growth, the parts that never touched soil. You can take cuttings from clean wood and graft them onto living stock, and they'll be the same trees, Malden's own stock, still fruiting somewhere.

The nearest living orchard is over the range, in Hillsbrad. It's a long way, over a mountain. I'm too old to carry them and too stubborn to let them die out there, so take them.
spn_orchard_graft.turn_in_text:
The Hillsbrad orchardman turns a cutting in the light and whistles.

That's old stock, proper old stock. We've got nothing like it this side of the range.

Tell your warden they've taken. Tell him we'll send word when they fruit, and tell him it'll be his orchard growing on our hill, which is a damn sight better than his orchard being nowhere at all.

spn_orchard_keeper.description:
He's under the big tree at the back. You'll have seen it and taken it for stump-work.

That was Malden's gardener. He spent forty years on that ground and knew every tree by name, and I mean that literally. He'd named them, and he'd use the names in conversation and look at you as if you were the strange one.

He's still working, and you need to understand that before you go down there. He prunes and clears windfall. He tends the blight the way he used to tend the crop, with exactly the same care, because as far as anything left in him is concerned the orchard is producing beautifully.

He gives a thin smile. He always did love his work.
spn_orchard_keeper.turn_in_text:
Malwick doesn't go and look.

I'll put him at the foot of the long row. He'd want to be in the ground out there, and now at least the ground can have him instead of the other way round.

And then I've got a proposition for you, if you've got the legs for a mountain.

spn_pell_glands.description:
You'll be the one Vesk keeps sending into the woods. I'm Apothecary Pell, and I've got a requisition and no one to requisition.

I want Silverpine spider venom. Properly cut and properly reduced, I believe it can be made to slow the Plague rather than feed it, which isn't a thing anyone in the Undercity wants to hear me say out loud.

I'll be honest with you, because you'll hear it from Vesk anyway. I've got a great many theories, and most of them have been wrong. This one can be tested with things that can be killed and weighed, rather than argued about in a chamber by people who've never cut anything.

Get me the glands. Bring them intact, if you can manage it, because a burst one is worth nothing but mess.
spn_pell_glands.turn_in_text:
They're all intact.

He's already weighing one.

Right, now I can be wrong about this properly, with figures, instead of being wrong about it hopefully.

spn_pools_beasts.description:
I'm Yaelis, the pools warden, and before you ask, yes, that was once a real posting. I've come down to the Sepulcher because a warden with no pools left to keep isn't much use up there.

The Shadowspring Pools were a drinking-hole. Forsaken went up there, stood at the water, and had an hour to themselves. There isn't much the risen want, but there's something about standing by water that a good many of us still do.

Then the springs turned black, the bog beasts came into the shallows, and the crocolisks came in after them. Now nobody stands at my pools at all.

I'd settle for making the near bank safe enough to stand beside. That isn't a strategic objective, and I'm aware of it. Clear the shallows anyway.
spn_pools_beasts.accept_text: Go to the shallows on the near bank. Take the bog beasts first, because the crocolisks follow them in.
spn_pools_beasts.turn_in_text:
Somebody told me they went up this evening and stood at the water for the better part of an hour.

They didn't say anything to me, and they didn't need to. That's the posting.

spn_pools_fangs.description:
Here's something you can actually be paid for, since I can't pay you.

The Rot Hide slitherers work the pools' edge, and their fangs carry a venom the Apothecary Society has standing coin out for. I mean properly standing coin. They'll take as many as anyone brings, and they've never once asked where from.

I want them drained for my own reasons, which are that a slitherer has taken two of my patrol in a year, and I'm not a big enough person to pretend that's professional detachment.

So you get the Society's coin, I get the pools' edge quieter, and the slitherers get what they've got coming. I find that an unusually tidy arrangement.
spn_pools_fangs.turn_in_text:
That's them drained and bagged.

Take the lot to the Society, and don't let them tell you the rate's dropped, because it hasn't. They say that to everyone who looks like they've walked a long way.

spn_ravenna_rite.description:
I'm Dark Cleric Ravenna. Come closer, because I won't raise my voice for this.

There's a woman at Olsen's Farthing called Marta. Her husband walks past her window every night, at the same hour, on the same track across the yard. He doesn't come to the door and he doesn't go away, and she's been watching it for a year and a half.

I've prepared a Rite of Quieting. It won't bring him back and it won't punish him. It'll let him stop. That's all it is, and that's all she asked for when she sent word.

I can't leave this gate. I've tried, and Vesk is right to stop me. So you'll take it. And listen to me: don't read it aloud on the road, not a line of it. The rite doesn't care where it's said.
spn_ravenna_rite.accept_text: Take it to Widow Marta at Olsen's Farthing, and don't read it aloud on the way.
spn_ravenna_rite.turn_in_text:
Marta holds the scroll without unrolling it.

He was a good walker. That's a stupid thing to say about a man, but it's what I keep thinking. He walked everywhere. He'd walk to the Sepulcher for a nail rather than wait for the cart.

I'll say it tonight at the hour he comes. Thank you for carrying it. And thank the cleric, and tell her I did ask, and nobody made me.

spn_rg_reckoning.description:
Stand there a moment. I want to do this properly.

There are four reports on this desk. The Watchman is down, Oswin's man, who'd been walking that round since before I had this post. The Scarecrow-King is down. The Orchardkeeper is down. Muckmaw is down, and I had a standing order about Muckmaw that I'd stopped expecting anyone to action.

That's four threads through these pines, and every one of them was somebody's year: Oswin's, Verrel's, Malwick's, Yaelis's. They've all written to me separately, and not one of them mentioned the others, because none of them knew there was a pattern. I'm the only one who sees all four.

So thank you, from this garrison, and from four people who'll never put it together.
spn_rg_reckoning.turn_in_text:
He actually stands up.

That's the Rear Guard's thanks, and it's worth exactly what the Rear Guard is worth, which these days isn't much.

But these pines are quieter than they were when you came up that road, and I keep the map, and the map says so.

spn_rh_husks.description:
I'm Keeper Oswin. You'll have to forgive the state of me. I've been digging since before light.

I've buried the same corpse three times this month. I know his face, I know which plot, and three times I've filled that hole in and three times he's been standing beside it in the morning with the soil off him.

The husks come up all over the back plots, faster than I can fill, which means I'm no longer a gravekeeper. I'm a man moving earth in a circle.

Thin them out for me. Give me one clear day. If I can get a full day's work done without it undoing itself behind me, I'll know this ground can still be kept.
spn_rh_husks.turn_in_text:
I had a whole day. I filled nine, and not one of them came back up.

He looks at his hands.

I'd stopped believing that was possible, which is a dangerous thing for a man in my trade to stop believing.

spn_rh_moss.description:
I'm Acolyte Dessa. Don't tread on the markers. That's not for reverence, it's for the moss.

Look at it. It only grows on the mourning stones. It doesn't grow on the walls, or the trees, or the ground between. It grows on the stones, and only the ones with names still legible on them, which is the detail that's kept me awake.

I think it feeds the dead, or they feed it. I've got the two possibilities written out, and I can't get further than that from the outside, because the creepers that tend it won't let me near a stone long enough to cut a clean sample.

Bring me clippings from the creepers themselves. Whatever they've been taking in is in them, and I'd very much like to know what this cemetery has been eating.
spn_rh_moss.turn_in_text:
She has three of them open before you've finished speaking.

It's the same in all of them. Whatever this is, it isn't local to a plot, it's local to the hill.

I'll need to say that to Oswin carefully. He's spent twenty years believing this is a graveyard with a problem, and I'm about to suggest it's a problem with a graveyard on it.

spn_rh_vigil.description:
I need to ask you for something tedious and a little frightening, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Something is lifting the dead on this hill. I don't mean raising them. I mean lifting them, from below, and if I knew where they were climbing from I'd know what I'm arguing with. The three oldest crypts are the only points on this hill where you can hear the under-ground properly.

So stand at each one. Stand still and listen, long enough to be certain of what you're hearing. That's all it is.

I've asked three people. None of them came back with an answer, and two of them came back.
spn_rh_vigil.accept_text: Find the three oldest crypts on Raven Hill: one east of me, one up the hill to the north, one down toward the Sepulcher road. Stand at each and listen properly, because it takes time.
spn_rh_vigil.turn_in_text:
Dessa listens to your description without interrupting once.

It's the same sound at all three, which means it isn't coming from a crypt at all. It's coming from under the whole hill, and they're the places thin enough to hear it.

Thank you. And I'm sorry. I'd hoped very much that you'd come back and tell me it was water.

spn_rh_watchman.description:
There's one walking the upper cemetery, and I'd rather you heard about him from me.

He's one of ours, a Forsaken watchman, posted here when Raven Hill still had a posting, and he's never stopped doing his rounds. It's the same route, at the same hours.

He doesn't answer a challenge any more, and I've tried. About a month ago I used his name, properly, the whole thing, the way you'd call to a man across a yard, and he turned and looked at me and there was nothing behind it, and then he carried on walking.

I knew him. He was better company than anyone else they ever sent up here. I'm not going to watch him walk that route through another winter.
spn_rh_watchman.turn_in_text:
Oswin takes a long time over it.

I'll put him up by the wall where he used to stop and look at the valley. He always stopped there, every round, at the same spot, and I never once asked him what he was looking at.

That's the part I'll be chewing on, more than the rest of it.

spn_scout_survey.description:
Don't stand in the road. Stand here, in the verge, where the ground's soft. That's why I'm standing in it.

Look at this, and this. There are fresh tracks on three spurs off the Trunk Road, all within a fortnight: the east road to the Dead Field, the path up to the Shadowspring Pools, and the lane into Malden's Orchard.

Three spurs is a pattern. One spur is somebody taking a short cut. Three is somebody mapping a wood. And every one of these goes off the road and doesn't come back onto it where I can see.

I want eyes on the far end of each, the ends, not the middles. Walk them to where they stop and tell me what's standing there.
spn_scout_survey.turn_in_text:
All three end somewhere occupied. I'd half hoped you'd come back and tell me I was reading deer.

I'll take this to Vesk tonight. He'll want it as three separate problems, and I'm going to make him look at it as one.

spn_sd_lair.description:
Here's the idea I wasn't ready to say.

Longleg came from somewhere. So did everything else in there, the size of them, the boldness, all of it starting at once a few months back. A wood doesn't change its mind like that. That's a brood with a mother in it.

There's a cave at the end of the Skittering road, the Widow's Lair, if you listen to the Crossroads carters. I've been to within sight of the mouth twice and turned back both times, and I'd like to stop pretending that was judgement.

Stand at the mouth. Don't go in. I mean that, don't go in. Tell me how deep the webs run and whether there's air moving out of it.
spn_sd_lair.accept_text: Go east along the Skittering road to the cave at its end, and stand at the mouth of the Widow's Lair. Don't go in.
spn_sd_lair.turn_in_text:
There's air coming out of it, warm air.

He's quiet for a while.

Then it isn't a cave, it's a way through to something, and this wood has been getting its weather from somewhere other than the sky.

That's beyond a webhunter. That goes to Vesk, and Vesk will send it on. And if you're going back into the Lair itself, see Bone-Carver Yseult. She's taken the rest of my list off me.

spn_sd_longleg.description:
Longleg is the one that takes a hunter a week.

It's the size of a cart. I want you to hold that in your head rather than nodding past it, because everyone nods past it, and then they see it and stop thinking clearly at exactly the wrong moment.

It doesn't web. It stalks, properly stalks. It matches your pace, stays off the path, and comes when you've stopped moving and started looking at something else. I've got three apprentices' worth of experience in that sentence, and I'd rather not get a fourth.

It'll be on the high ground off the Skittering road. Go slowly, don't stop in the open, and don't look at anything for long.
spn_sd_longleg.turn_in_text:
Corvane sits down on the path, which in this wood isn't something he does.

That was three apprentices.

I'll take their kit down to the Crossroads and send it on. I've been carrying it in my pack for a year, because sending it felt like finishing something.

spn_sd_sacs.description:
Now the part that actually ends it, rather than postponing it.

The skitterers carry their egg sacs with them. They don't nest them and they don't leave them. They carry them, which is why nobody has ever found a chamber to burn, and why everyone who's tried to clear that wood has failed doing it the sensible way.

Take the sacs off them, all you can carry.

And here's the other thing, and it's why I want them rather than just destroyed in place. The Widow's brood will follow a sac, and they'll follow it a long way. A man holding enough of them can make something in this wood listen to him, and I've got an idea about that which I'm not ready to say out loud yet.
spn_sd_sacs.turn_in_text:
He stows them with a great deal more care than he's shown anything else.

That's the next generation in a bag instead of in the wood.

Don't ask me yet. Ask me after Longleg.

spn_sd_skitterers.description:
When you go into the Skittering Dark, keep to the middle of the path and don't put a hand out to steady yourself. Everything in there that looks like a branch is a decision.

I'm Corvane, the webhunter. I've worked the Skittering Dark for months, and I'll tell you what's changed, because it's changed fast. They're bigger, they're bolder, and they've started drifting toward the Trunk Road.

That last one is what matters. A spider in a wood is a spider in a wood. A spider on a supply road is a Sepulcher problem with my name on the report.

Cull the breeding stock, the big skitterers and the full-grown ones. Take them before the swarm rather than after, because after is a different conversation entirely.
spn_sd_skitterers.turn_in_text:
That's a dent in the next generation.

They'll breed it back if we stop. That's the whole miserable arithmetic of this wood. You don't win, you just stay ahead.

spn_trunk_walk.description:
I'm Captain Vesk, of the Forsaken Rear Guard. This gate is the border, and that road is the only reason the gate matters.

The Trunk Road runs from here to the Crossroads and on to the Sepulcher. Everything we have in Silverpine comes up it: orders, relief, the carts, the occasional person who actually knows something. Cut the road, and this garrison stops being a border post and becomes a building full of men in a wood.

Nobody has walked the whole length of it since the first frost. We patrol the first mile and the Sepulcher patrols their end, and in between there's a stretch that exists on my map and nowhere else.

Walk all of it, to the Crossroads. Then come back and tell me what my map is wrong about.
spn_trunk_walk.turn_in_text:
Vesk marks three places on the map while you talk, and he doesn't like any of them.

So it's passable, passable and watched.

That's worth knowing, and I'd rather not have learned it. Thank you. You're the first man to give me that road in months.

spn_worg_cull.description:
Now you've walked it, you'll have seen the verge.

The worgs have moved onto it. They aren't in the road. They're on the verge, the strip of scrub either side, where a thing can pace a cart for half a mile without ever being in the open. That's hunting behaviour, and it's new this season.

And the ghouls have come in behind them, because a worg pack leaves a great deal behind and a ghoul isn't proud. So now there are two problems on that strip, and the second exists entirely because of the first.

Push them both back out of range of the road. Start with the worgs. Take their leavings away, and the ghouls will follow the food elsewhere.
spn_worg_cull.accept_text: Go along the verge of the Trunk Road, both sides. Take the worgs first.
spn_worg_cull.turn_in_text:
The verge is clear enough to see across, which is all I ever ask of a verge.

That'll hold until the frost pushes them back down. By then I'd like to have a proper patrol on this stretch instead of borrowing passing strangers.
